subject: playwright
title: Debugging flaky tests
description: Reading a trace, what retries really tell you, and the difference between a flaky test and a flaky application.

content.title: The trace is the evidence
content.body: A trace records every action with a DOM snapshot before and after, the network log, the console and a screencast. On a CI-only failure it is the difference between reproducing for an afternoon and seeing, in thirty seconds, that the click landed on a cookie banner.

content.title: Capture it where it matters
content.body: on-first-retry is the default worth keeping: no cost on green runs, a full trace the moment something fails.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: A test that only passes on retry is not fixed. Retries buy a green pipeline and hide either a real race in the product or a real assumption in the test — the flaky count in the report is the number that matters.

exercises.question: Which of these is NOT in a Playwright trace?

answers.text: A DOM snapshot before and after each action
The network requests the page made
A live, interactive copy of the application you can click through
Console messages and the test's source location

exercises.explanation: Snapshots are inspectable with dev tools but frozen — nothing re-executes. That is exactly why they are trustworthy evidence of what the page looked like at that moment.

exercises.question: Complete the command that opens a downloaded trace from a CI artifact.

answers.text: show-trace
open-trace
trace
view

exercises.explanation: It runs entirely locally — no server, no re-run of the test. trace.playwright.dev does the same in a browser tab if you would rather not download the CLI.

exercises.question: A test reported as "flaky" failed at least once and then passed on a retry.
exercises.explanation: The reporter separates flaky from failed for exactly this reason. Treat the flaky column as a backlog, not as noise.

exercises.question: Which line will make this test hang forever in CI?

answers.text: Line 1 — goto needs waitUntil
Line 3 — toHaveCount does not exist
Line 2 — page.pause() waits for a human in the Inspector
Nothing — pause is a no-op in headless mode

exercises.explanation: It is a debugging aid, not a wait. Lint for it, or it eventually costs someone a whole pipeline timeout.

exercises.question: A test fails only on CI, never locally. Which difference is worth checking first?

answers.text: Viewport size, timezone, locale and machine speed — CI defaults differ from your machine
The Playwright version, which is pinned anyway
The operating system, which never affects the DOM
Nothing — CI-only failures are always infrastructure

exercises.explanation: A narrower viewport collapses a menu behind a hamburger; a different timezone shifts a date label. Pin viewport, locale and timezoneId in the config so both environments agree.

exercises.question: Complete the environment variable that opens the Inspector and steps through the run.

answers.text: PWDEBUG
DEBUG
PLAYWRIGHT_DEBUG
PW_INSPECT

exercises.explanation: PWDEBUG=1 opens the Inspector, disables timeouts and runs headed. DEBUG=pw:api is the other one worth knowing — it logs every API call to the terminal.

exercises.question: What does test.step add?

answers.text: A named, collapsible group in the report and the trace, with its own duration
A retry boundary — only the step is retried
A separate browser context for those actions
Nothing at runtime; it is only a comment

exercises.explanation: Steps make a long trace readable and tell you which phase got slow. They do not change execution or retry semantics.

exercises.question: A test intermittently clicks a button a moment before the handler is attached. What is the honest diagnosis?

answers.text: A real product issue — the control looks interactive before it is
A test issue; add a short waitForTimeout
A Playwright issue with actionability
A CI issue; increase the worker count

exercises.explanation: Playwright reproduced a race a fast user could hit too. The fix belongs in the app — disable the button until it is wired — and the test then documents it.

exercises.question: Playwright · CLI
exercises.back: Runs the same test twenty times in parallel — the quickest way to confirm a flake
exercises.explanation: Pair it with --grep to narrow to one test. If twenty runs are green, the flake is probably environmental rather than in the test.

exercises.question: trace: 'on' is a good default for a large CI suite.
exercises.explanation: It records every test, which slows the run and produces artifacts measured in gigabytes. on-first-retry gives you a trace exactly for the runs you want to look at.

exercises.question: This suite is green with retries: 2 and red with retries: 0. What does that tell you?

answers.text: The retry timeout is too short
Nothing — that is what retries are for
The test depends on data another test creates, and only passes once that test has run
toBeVisible needs a longer timeout

exercises.explanation: A retry re-runs the test later, by which time the other test has produced the invoice. The suite is order-dependent; the retry is just hiding it.

exercises.question: What does this do?

answers.text: Adds the payload to the HTML report and the trace for that test
Sends it to the reporter's remote endpoint
Writes it to the console on failure
Stores it for comparison on the next run

exercises.explanation: Attachments are the cheapest way to make a CI failure diagnosable: the exact response, id or seed the run used, sitting next to the trace.
